candidates.statement: The International Council for Harmonisation (ICH) guidance for industry Q12 Technical and 17 Regulatory Considerations for Pharmaceutical Product Lifecycle Management and its Annexes 18 (ICH Q12, May 2021) provide a framework to facilitate the management of postapproval 19 chemistry, manufacturing, and controls (CMC) changes in a more predictable and efficient 20 manner. 2 ICH Q12 includes regulatory tools and enablers with associated guiding principles that 21 should enhance industry’s ability to manage postapproval changes and increase transparency 22 between industry and regulatory authorities, supporting innovation and continual improvement. 23
candidates.context: This guidance should be read in conjunction with ICH Q12, which this guidance complements 25 by clarifying how the ICH Q12 tools and enablers can be implemented within the U.S. regulatory 26 system. These guidances apply to drug substances and drug products 3 that are the subject of new 27 drug applications (NDAs), biologics license applications (BLAs), abbreviated new drug 28 applications (ANDAs), and supplements to these applications regulated by the Center for Drug 29 Evaluation and Research (CDER) and the Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research 30 (CBER). They also apply to combination products 4 with device constituent parts that are the 31 subject of NDAs, BLAs, ANDAs, and supplements to these applications regulated by CDER and 32 CBER. 33

candidates.statement: ICH Q12 describes two categories for regulatory communications: prior approval and 58 notification. In the U.S. regulatory system, prior approval means a prior approval supplement 59 (PAS), notification moderate means a changes being effected-30 (CBE-30) supplement, and 60 notification low means a CBE-0 supplement or annual report. 5 As indicated in ICH Q12, the 61 lowest risk changes are managed and documented within the pharmaceutical quality system 62 (PQS) and do not need to be reported, but they may be verified during a surveillance or other 63 inspection. 64
candidates.context: B. Categorization of Postapproval CMC Changes 56 C. Established Conditions 66

candidates.statement: ICH Q12 defines established conditions (ECs) as legally binding information considered 68 necessary to assure product quality. As a consequence, any change to ECs necessitates a 69 submission to the regulatory authority. This is consistent with FDA’s regulations at 21 CFR 70 314.70(a)(1)(i), 314.97(a), and 601.12(a)(1). Although these regulations do not explicitly specify 71 what constitutes an EC, they do set forth a risk-based paradigm for reporting changes. In 72 addition, existing FDA guidance documents describe a broad set of postapproval changes and 73 make recommendations for how they should be reported. 6 The risk-based paradigm set forth in 74 the regulations and the recommendations in these associated guidance documents can help 75

candidates.statement: For each proposed EC, the applicant may identify a proposed reporting category: PAS, CBE-30, 175 CBE-0, or annual report. If this reporting category differs from that recommended in existing 176 guidance, the applicant should provide a justification in the relevant section of module 3. This 177 justification can be part of or complementary to the justification provided to support 178 identification of the EC. If the applicant chooses not to propose reporting categories, the 179 applicant should include a statement that reporting categories for changes to those ECs will 180 follow the regulations and the recommendations in guidance. 181

candidates.statement: If information about the drug substance or drug product is incorporated in an application by 186 reference to a Type II drug master file (DMF), 10 ECs associated with that drug substance or drug 187 product can be proposed, but they should only be proposed as part of the application. 11 In such 188 cases, the DMF holder will need to share sufficient information with the applicant 12 so that 189 proposed ECs and their associated reporting categories can be specified in and approved as part 190 of the application. The justification in support of the identification of ECs can be located in the 191 DMF, as long as the application refers to the specific location of the justification in the DMF. 192 The applicant should provide a justification for proposed reporting categories in the application 193 because the justification will generally be specific to the final drug product and its conditions of 194 approval (e.g., dosing, route of administration) rather than generalizable across different products 195

candidates.statement: Applicants may propose ECs for the device constituent part of a combination product in an 204 NDA, BLA, or ANDA. The combination product as a whole, including the roles and interactions 205 of the constituent parts, should be considered in proposing ECs and reporting categories for the 206 product, including in relation to each constituent part. The focus of this section is identifying 207 ECs for device constituent parts in particular. One approach is to assess the “characteristics of 208 the product that are essential for its safe and proper use” 13 (primary characteristics) relating to 209 the device constituent part and to identify the associated ECs. The primary characteristics for the 210 device constituent part of a combination product generally include: 211

candidates.statement: As indicated in ICH Q12, maintenance of the application is subject to regional requirements. To 272 ensure that FDA has access to up-to-date analytical procedures, applicants should include in the 273 annual report a copy of all analytical procedures that have been appropriately modified during 274 the reporting period without a submission (i.e., managed only through the PQS as changes did 275 not relate to ECs). This information is intended to be for information only and typically is not 276 subject to review unless it is determined that changes to ECs for the procedure were in fact made. 277 Applicants should include this information in eCTD section 1.13.5 or 1.13.7 with a statement 278 such as “For information only: Changes made to analytical methods, including those not 279 requiring submission.” 280

candidates.statement: As described in ICH Q12, the PLCM document should include proposed ECs, reporting 300 categories for making changes to approved ECs, a list of comparability protocols (if submitted), 301 and postapproval CMC commitments, if applicable. FDA recommends that the PLCM document 302 be provided in tabular format in eCTD section 3.2.R, with specific references to the submission 303 sequence, eCTD section number, and page number where each EC’s scientific justification can 304 be found. FDA further recommends that the PLCM indicate the manufacturing sites (preferably 305 by facility establishment identifier (FEI) number) where an EC will be implemented. 15 For 306 example, if there are two drug product manufacturing sites named in the application, but the 307 manufacturing process-related ECs will only be associated with the manufacturing at one of 308 those two sites, the FEI number of this site should be specified in the PLCM for those process- 309 related ECs. It is then assumed that ECs for operations at the other facility will follow the 310 regulations and the recommendations in guidance. If the ECs will be implemented at both sites, 311 both FEI numbers should be listed. Applicants should attribute FEIs to ECs in the PLCM at the 312 most inclusive level (e.g., one FEI listed at the beginning of 3.2.P if all subsequent ECs in the 313 section are associated with one drug product facility). See appendix C in this guidance for an 314 example of a PLCM document. 315

candidates.statement: As indicated in ICH Q12, in addition to compliance with current good manufacturing practice 323 (CGMP) requirements, 16 an effective PQS is necessary to support the use of the tools in that 324 guidance. However, also as noted in that guidance, FDA will not require a specific inspection 325 before an applicant can make use of the principles in the guidance. FDA’s assessment of the 326 effectiveness of the PQS will generally be informed by routine inspections conducted by FDA 327 and capable foreign regulators 17 and other available information. Management should employ 328 the principles of ICH guidance for industry Q10 Pharmaceutical Quality System (April 2009) to 329 ensure the continued capability of the PQS to support the management of ECs. 330

candidates.statement: As indicated in ICH Q12, inspection observations that raise concern regarding the effectiveness 350 of the PQS, and change management in particular, may lead to a need to modify previously 351 approved ECs, reporting categories, or comparability protocols until such time as the PQS 352 effectiveness has returned to an acceptable state. In these cases, FDA intends to communicate the 353 impact of such findings on previously approved ECs, reporting categories, and comparability 354 protocols with facilities and applicants, as appropriate. 355
candidates.context: FDA will also consider information included in a supplement that supports a determination that 342 the new site deserves the same level of regulatory flexibility regarding postapproval changes as 343 the site included in the original application. The determination of PQS capability will consider 344 factors such as whether the new site is operated under the same PQS as the original; the state of 345 regulatory compliance determined by FDA and other national drug regulatory authorities; 346 conformance with ICH Q10, especially as concerns change management practices; and 347 conformance with other applicable change management regulations and policies. 348 G.
